passages.original: Pater æternus eo quod æternum habeat Filium , cujus æternus sit Pater: Filius artius, en quod sit Patri coæternus : Spirit is sanctus æternus, co quod sit Patri et Filio coæternus. Non confusa in una persona Trinitas, ut Sabellius dicit: neque separata aut divisa I in natura divinitas, ut Arius blasphemat : sed alter in persona Patcr, alter in persona Filius, alter in persona Spiritus sanctus; unus natura' in sancta Trinitate Deus Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus.
passages.english: The Father is eternal because he has an eternal Son, of whom he is the eternal Father; the Son is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father; the Holy Spirit is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Son. The Trinity is not confused into one person, as Sabellius says; nor is the divinity separated or divided in nature, as Arius blasphemes; but the Father is one in person, the Son another in person, the Holy Spirit another in person; in the holy Trinity the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God in nature.
passages.notes: "artius, en" is read as "æternus, eo"; "Spirit is" as "Spiritus"; "co" as "eo".

passages.original: non naturæ versibilitate, sicut Apollinaristae dicunt, sed Dei dignatione : ut nec Deus mutaretur in humanam substantiam assumendo hominem, nec homo in divinam glorilicatus in Deum : quia mutatio vel versibilitas naturæ et diminutionem ct abolitionem substantiæ facit 1. Natus est ergo Dei Filius ex homine, non per hominem, id est, non ex viri coitu, sicut Ebion dicit: sed carnem ex Virginis corpore trahens , et non de coelo secum afferens, sicut Marcion, Origenes ei EutychIs alfirmant 2. Neque in phantasia, id est, ahsque carne , sicut Valentinus : neque δοϰήσει(a), id est , ncquc putative imaginatum ; sed corpus verum; non tantum carnem ex carne, sicut Marcianus;
passages.english: not by a changeability of nature, as the Apollinarists say, but by God's condescension, so that neither was God changed into human substance by assuming man, nor was man, glorified into God, [changed] into the divine [substance]; for change or changeability of nature brings about both the diminution and the abolition of the substance. The Son of God, then, was born from a human being, not through a human being, that is, not from intercourse with a man, as Ebion says; but drawing [his] flesh from the Virgin's body, and not bringing it with him from heaven, as Marcion, Origen and Eutyches assert. Nor [was he] in appearance, that is, without flesh, as Valentinus [says]; nor by *dokēsis* (seeming), that is, imagined as if only supposed; but [he had] a true body; not only flesh from flesh, as Marcianus [says];
passages.notes: "Marcianus" is uncertain; possibly a corruption (e.g. for Marcion or another name).

passages.original: CAPUT IV. — (b) Nihil erratum aut serviens in Trinitate credendum, ut vult Dionysius fons Arii : nihil inæquale, ut Eunomius : nihil æquale a gratia, ut vult Aetius : nihil anterius posteriusve ant minus, ut Arins : nihil extraneum aut officiale alteri, ut Macedonius : nihil pervasione 4 aut surreptione insertum , ut Manichæus : nihil corporcum , ut Melito et Tertullianus : nihil corporaliter effigiatum, nt Anthropomorphus I et Vadianus : nihil sibi invisibile 6 ut Origenes, : nihil creaturis visihile, ut Fortunatus : nihil moribus vel voluntate diversum , ut Marcion : nihil ex Trinitatis essentia ad creaturarum naturam deductum , ut Plato et Tertullianus : nihil officio singulare nee alteri communicabile, ut Origenes : nihil confusum , ut Sabellius : sed totum perlectum ; quia totum ex uno et unum 1 : non tamen solitarium , ut præsumunt Praxeas et Sylvanus , Pentapolitana damnabilis illa doctrina.
passages.english: CHAPTER IV. — Nothing created or serving is to be believed in the Trinity, as Dionysius, the source of Arius, would have it; nothing unequal, as Eunomius [holds]; nothing equal by grace, as Aetius would have it; nothing earlier or later or lesser, as Arius [holds]; nothing foreign or subservient to another, as Macedonius [holds]; nothing inserted by invasion or stealth, as Manichaeus [holds]; nothing bodily, as Melito and Tertullian [hold]; nothing given bodily shape, as the Anthropomorphite and Audianus [hold]; nothing invisible to itself, as Origen [holds]; nothing visible to creatures, as Fortunatus [holds]; nothing differing in character or will, as Marcion [holds]; nothing drawn from the essence of the Trinity into the nature of creatures, as Plato and Tertullian [hold]; nothing singular in function and not communicable to another, as Origen [holds]; nothing confused, as Sabellius [holds]; but the whole is perfect, because the whole is from one and [is] one; not, however, solitary, as Praxeas and Sylvanus presume, that damnable Pentapolitan doctrine.
passages.notes: "erratum" read as "creatum"; "Vadianus" taken as Audianus (Audius); "perlectum" as "perfectum".

passages.original: — Erit resurrectio mortuorum omnium, sed una et insimul et semel : non prima justorum , et secunda peccatorum , ut fabula est somniatorum a; sed una omnium. Et si id resurgere dicitur quod cadit, caro ergo nostra in veritalc resurget, sicut in veritate cadit. Et non secundum Origenem immutatio corporum erit, id est, aliud novum corpus pro carne : sed eadem caro corruptibilis quæ cadit, tam justorum quam injustorum, incorruptibilis resurget, que vel poenam sufferre possit pro peccatis, vel in gloria æterna manere pro mcritis.
passages.english: There will be a resurrection of all the dead, but one, all together and once: not a first [resurrection] of the righteous and a second of sinners, as is the tale of dreamers, but one of all. And if what is said to rise is that which falls, then our flesh will rise in truth, just as it falls in truth. And the change of bodies will not be according to Origen, that is, another new body in place of the flesh; but the same corruptible flesh which falls, of the righteous as much as of the unrighteous, will rise incorruptible, so that it may either endure punishment for sins or remain in eternal glory for merits.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'veritalc' to 'veritate', 'mcritis' to 'meritis'; stray footnote mark 'a' omitted. 'que' read as 'quae'.

passages.original: CAPUT VIII. — Quod autem dicimus in Symbolo, in adventu Domini vivos ac mortuos judicandos, non solum justos et peccatores significari, sicut Diodorus putat, sed et vivos eos qui in carne inveniendi sunt credimus, qui adhuc morituri creduntur; vel immulandi sunt, ut alii volunt, ut suscitati continuo vel reformati cum ante mortuis judicemur.
passages.english: Chapter VIII. Now as for what we say in the Creed, that at the coming of the Lord the living and the dead are to be judged, we believe that not only the righteous and sinners are meant, as Diodorus thinks, but also the living, those who are to be found in the flesh, who are believed still to be going to die; or [who] are to be changed, as others hold, so that, raised at once or re-formed, we may be judged together with those who died before.
passages.notes: 'immulandi' read as 'immutandi'. Diodorus is presumably Diodore of Tarsus.

passages.original: CAPUT XVI. — Salum hominem credimus habere animam substantivam , quæ exula corpore vivit, et sensus suos atque ingenia vivaciter tenet. Neque cum . corpore moritur , sicut Aratus 4 asserit : neque post modicum intervallum , sicut Zenon dicit; quia substantialiter vivit.
passages.english: Chapter XVI. We believe that man alone has a substantial soul, which lives when released from the body and keeps its senses and faculties in full vigour. Nor does it die with the body, as Aratus asserts, nor after a short interval, as Zeno says; for it lives substantially.
passages.notes: 'Salum' read as 'Solum', 'exula' as 'exuta'; footnote mark '4' omitted. 'Aratus' is uncertain; other witnesses may read a different name (e.g. Arabs/Arabici).

passages.original: CAPUT XVII. — Ammalium vero aniMa! non sunt substantivæ 8, sed cum carne ipsa carnis vivacitate nascuntur, et cum carnis morte finiuntur : et ideo nec ratione reguntur, sicut Plato ct Alexander putant, sed ad omnia naturne incitamento ducuntur.
passages.english: Chapter XVII. The souls of animals, however, are not substantial, but are born with the flesh itself through the vitality of the flesh, and end with the death of the flesh; and therefore they are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander think, but are led to everything by the prompting of nature.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'Ammalium vero aniMa!' to 'Animalium vero animae', 'ct' to 'et', 'naturne' to 'naturae'; footnote mark '8' omitted. The Alexander meant is not certain (perhaps Alexander of Aphrodisias).

passages.original: Procliani, Borboritæ, Siphori, qui nunc vocantur Bonosiani, Photiniani, Montanitæ et Manichæi, varia impiclatis gcrmina : vel cæteræ istorum originis sive ordinis pestes, quæ duo principia sibi ignota introducunt, ut Cerdon et Marcion; vel contraria, ut Manichæus ; vel tria et barbara , ut Selianns cl Theodosius 4 ; vel multa , ut ValentinuS ; vel Christum hominem fuisse abs que Deo, ut Cerinthus, Ebion, Artemon et Photinus. Ex iatis, inquam, si qui ad nos venerint, non requirendum ab eis utrum baptizati sint, an non;
passages.english: the Proclians, Borborites, Siphori (who are now called Bonosians), Photinians, Montanists and Manichaeans, various offshoots of impiety; or the other plagues of their origin or order, who introduce two principles unknown to each other, as Cerdo and Marcion; or opposed [principles], as Manichaeus; or three, and barbarous ones, as Selianus and Theodosius; or many, as Valentinus; or [who hold] that Christ was a man without God, as Cerinthus, Ebion, Artemon and Photinus. If any of these, I say, come to us, they are not to be asked whether they have been baptised or not;
passages.notes: "Siphori" and "Selianus" are uncertain names (Selianus perhaps for Seleucus or Sethianus).
